      <title>Six npm Packages Use Ethereum Transactions to Retrieve Malicious Payloads</title>
      <link>https://www.sonatype.com/blog/six-npm-packages-use-ethereum-transactions-to-retrieve-malicious-payloads</link>
      <description><div class="hs-featured-image-wrapper"> 
 <a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/six-npm-packages-use-ethereum-transactions-to-retrieve-malicious-payloads" title="" class="hs-featured-image-link"> <img src="https://www.sonatype.com/hubfs/RapidResponse_Contagious%20Interview.png" alt="Image with text: &quot;Breaking news, Sonatype Research identified sonatype-2026-005899, DPRK 'Contagious Interview'&quot;" class="hs-featured-image" style="width:auto !important; max-width:50%; float:left; margin:0 15px 15px 0;"> </a> 
</div> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">TL;DR</h2> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p><span>Sonatype Research Labs identified six npm packages delivering the same malicious payload: three hijacked legitimate packages and three additional malicious packages, tracked as </span><a href="https://guide.sonatype.com/vulnerability/sonatype-2026-005899" style="text-decoration: none;"><span style="color: #188038;">sonatype-2026-005899</span></a><span> and </span><a href="https://guide.sonatype.com/vulnerability/sonatype-2026-005901" style="text-decoration: none;"><span style="color: #188038;">sonatype-2026-005901</span></a><span>.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p>The malware uses the same Ethereum wallet addr<span style="text-decoration: none;">ess </span><a href="https://opensourcemalware.com/blog/nullreceiver-dprk-c2-technique" style="text-decoration: none;">identified by OpenSourceMalware</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> in a</span>ctivity attributed to the DPRK-linked Contagious Interview campaign, using the "NullReceiver"&nbsp;technique to locate infrastructure hosting additional JavaScript payloads.</p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Organizations that installed the affected versions should remove them and investigate the impacted environment for follow-on payload execution or compromise.</span></p> </li> 
</ul> 
<p><span>On August 10, 2026, Sonatype Research Labs identified six npm packages containing the same malicious payload, including three compromised legitimate packages and three packages published with the malware already present.</span></p> 
<p><span>The payload uses Ethereum blockchain transactions to locate infrastructure hosting additional JavaScript malware. Sonatype researchers confirmed the six packages use the same Ethereum wallet address in recent activity attributed to the DPRK-linked Contagious Interview campaign. OpenSourceMalware dubbed the specific blockchain-based command-and-control technique "NullReceiver,"&nbsp;while Contagious Interview refers to the broader campaign associated with the Lazarus APT group.</span></p> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">Six npm Packages Deliver the Same Malware</h2> 
<p><span>According to Sonatype's Adam Reynolds, the affected packages fall into two groups.</span></p> 
<p><span>Three are legitimate npm packages that appear to have been hijacked to publish malicious versions, which Sonatype is tracking as </span><span style="color: #188038;">sonatype-2026-005899</span><span>:</span></p> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p><span style="color: #188038;">@kolbo/mcp@1.57.1</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span style="color: #188038;">agentgui@1.0.1127</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span style="color: #188038;">godot-kit@1.0.1786316795</span></p> </li> 
</ul> 
<p><span>In the hijacked packages, the payload was embedded into a file that already existed in the legitimate package, pictured here in the last line of database.js in </span><span style="color: #188038;">agentgui</span><span>.</span></p> 
<p> <span style="font-size: 1rem;">Researchers later identified three additional npm packages carrying the same payload, tracked separately as </span><span style="color: #188038;">sonatype-2026-005901</span><span style="font-size: 1rem;"> as they aren't package hijackings:</span></p> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p><span style="color: #188038;">envpack-conf@1.0.1</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span style="color: #188038;">postcss-initial-provider@3.0.4</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span style="color: #188038;">tailwindcss-motion-advanced@1.0.1</span></p> </li> 
</ul> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">Why This Malware Looks to the Blockchain for Its Next Move</h2> 
<p><span>Despite the different paths into npm, all six packages contain the same malicious payload and are associated with the same wallet address.</span></p> 
<p><span>When executed, the loader queries Ethereum for an outbound transaction from that wallet and reads bytes from the transaction’s recipient address. Those bytes are decoded into two IPv4 addresses, which the malware treats as primary and secondary command-and-control (C2) endpoints. The Ethereum transaction acts as a dead drop for instructions telling the malware where to connect next.</span></p> 
<p>The implementation Sonatype observed is also more extensive than t<span style="text-decoration: none;">he </span><a href="https://opensourcemalware.com/blog/nullreceiver-dprk-c2-technique" style="text-decoration: none;">NullReceiver</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> be</span>havior. The loader can query several Ethereum RPC providers, race requests between them, use batched JSON-RPC calls, and fall back to the Blockscout API to locate the relevant transaction. This gives the malware multiple ways to recover its C2 infrastructure if one method fails.</p> 
<p><span>Once it resolves the C2 infrastructure, the loader attempts to retrieve two additional stages from the /0x/cls and /0x/ls endpoints. It can retrieve an encoded payload through a standard HTTP GET response or, if that fails, make a HEAD request and recover it from an X-Payload-B64 response header. The payload is then Base64- and XOR-decoded before execution. The payload retrieved from /0x/cls can be executed directly in the current Node.js process using eval(), while downloaded stages can also be launched as detached Node.js child processes.</span></p> 
<h2 style="font-weight: normal; font-size: 30px;">Same Payload, Two Paths Into npm</h2> 
<p><span>The six packages show the same malware being distributed in two different ways: by compromising packages developers may already trust, and by publishing new packages created specifically to deliver the malicious payload.</span></p> 
<p><span>In the three hijacked packages, substantial legitimate functionality remains intact, with the malicious loader appended to the end of a legitimate file, which is the same behavior we saw with the DPRK-linked </span><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/hijacked-npm-package-attempts-to-deliver-polinrider-linked-rat?__hstc=45788219.e059ff2a8ab914cb2d79bf48cb86863e.1786377217886.1786377217886.1786377217886.1&amp;__hssc=45788219.1.1786377217886&amp;__hsfp=c89e5f7cdda40da39c08dc60049b9ac9" style="text-decoration: none;">PolinRider campaign</a><span>.</span></p> 
<p><span>The independently published packages also contain legitimate-looking functionality: </span><span style="color: #188038;">envpack-conf</span><span> includes package-configuration code, </span><span style="color: #188038;">postcss-initial-provider</span><span> includes normal PostCSS plugin code, and </span><span style="color: #188038;">tailwindcss-motion-advanced</span><span> carries the loader inside utils.min.js.</span></p> 
<h2 style="font-weight: normal; font-size: 30px;">A Familiar DPRK-Linked Technique</h2> 
<p><span>The six packages use a technique that closely resembles </span><strong><span>NullReceiver</span></strong><span>, a blockchain-based command-and-control method used in the DPRK-linked Contagious Interview campaign, recently spotted by </span><a href="https://opensourcemalware.com/blog/nullreceiver-dprk-c2-technique" style="text-decoration: none;">OpenSourceMalware</a><span> in two npm packages, </span><span style="color: #188038;">bianira-ui</span><span> and </span><span style="color: #188038;">fluid-type-ui</span><span>. </span></p> 
<p><span>In that activity, the malware looked up an attacker-controlled Ethereum wallet, read the recipient address from its latest outbound transaction, decoded a C2 IP from that address, and then connected to it. OpenSourceMalware attributed those packages to the DPRK Contagious Interview campaign.</span></p> 
<p><span>Sonatype Research Labs observed similar tradecraft here: hijacked packages, blockchain-based retrieval of follow-on infrastructure, and malicious code embedded into or shipped with package files.</span></p> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">Check Your Builds for These Six npm Packages</h2> 
<p><span>Developers and security teams should check their environments for the six affected npm packages and remove any impacted versions.</span></p> 
<p><span>For the three hijacked packages, the risk is especially easy to miss because the malicious code arrived through packages developers may already recognize and trust. The three additional malicious packages show the same payload can also be introduced through newly published packages.</span></p> 
<p><span>If any affected package was installed, teams should investigate for follow-on JavaScript execution and other signs of compromise.</span></p> 
<p><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/sonatype-research-labs" style="text-decoration: none;">Sonatype Research Labs</a> is continuing to investigate related npm activity and will update its findings as additional packages or infrastructure are identified.</p></description>

      <title>Flooding Dropper Hits npm With 850 Malicious Packages</title>
      <link>https://www.sonatype.com/blog/flooding-dropper-hits-npm-with-850-malicious-packages</link>
      <description><div class="hs-featured-image-wrapper"> 
 <a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/flooding-dropper-hits-npm-with-850-malicious-packages" title="" class="hs-featured-image-link"> <img src="https://www.sonatype.com/hubfs/RapidResponse_Flooding%20Dropper%20V3.png" alt="Image with text &quot;Breaking news: Sonatype Research indentified sonatype-2026-005660, new 'flooding dropper' campaign &quot;" class="hs-featured-image" style="width:auto !important; max-width:50%; float:left; margin:0 15px 15px 0;"> </a> 
</div> 
<h2 style="font-weight: normal; font-size: 30px;">TL;DR</h2> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p>Sonatype Research Labs is tracking an active malicious package campaign, dubbed 'Flooding Dropper,'&nbsp;spreading on npm, <a href="https://guide.sonatype.com/vulnerability/sonatype-2026-005660/sonatype-research" style="text-decoration: none;">currently impacting 846 software components</a><span>.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>The attacker appears to be automating parts of the npm account and package creation process, combining terms such as bigops and bnpl with other words and recurring version patterns, such as releases in the 35.x.y range.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>When installed, the packages download and execute a second-stage payload, using multiple delivery methods to improve the attack's chances of success.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Sonatype is tracking this campaign as </span><a href="https://guide.sonatype.com/vulnerability/sonatype-2026-005660/sonatype-research" style="text-decoration: none;">sonatype-2026-005660</a><span>. Impacted organizations should consider the host compromised, remove the package, investigate secondary payload execution and persistence, and rotate exposed credentials only after the environment has been cleaned.</span></p> </li> 
</ul> 
<p><span>On August 5, 2026, security researchers from OpenSourceMalware </span><a href="https://opensourcemalware.com/npm/bigops-backend" style="text-decoration: none;">reported a malicious npm package named bigops-backend</a><span> that delivered a platform-specific binary to Windows, Linux, and macOS systems.</span></p> 
<p><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/sonatype-research-labs" style="text-decoration: none;">Sonatype Research Labs</a>' Jorge Cardona observed this package is part of a much larger, ongoing campaign. At the time of publication, Sonatype has identified 846 software components implicated in the campaign, dubbed 'Flooding Dropper.'</p> 
<p><span>Rather than relying on a single publisher, the campaign generates npm accounts and publishes small numbers of packages from each one. Many package names interpolate terms such as bigops and bnpl, including examples resembling:</span></p> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p><span>bigops-api</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>dolyame-boxy-desktop-bnpl-card-gallery</span></p> </li> 
</ul>

 <li> <p><span>Attempts to download the binary from a randomized set of hardcoded remote hosts.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Falls back to DNS TXT records if the direct HTTPS downloads fail.</span></p> </li>

 <li> <p><span>Checking for debuggers, virtual machines, sandboxes, and security products and copying itself to a persistent location under the user’s AppData directory.</span></p> </li>

 <li> <p><span>Review process, DNS, proxy, and endpoint telemetry for payload retrieval.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Investigate detached processes originating from Node.js, npm, or temporary directories.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Identify any subsequent executables or in-memory payloads.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Remove persistence and rebuild affected systems when appropriate.</span></p> </li>

      <title>Mini Shai-Hulud npm Attack: More Than 2,200 Components Impacted</title>
      <link>https://www.sonatype.com/blog/mini-shai-hulud-npm-attack-more-than-2200-components-impacted</link>
      <description><div class="hs-featured-image-wrapper"> 
 <a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/mini-shai-hulud-npm-attack-more-than-2200-components-impacted" title="" class="hs-featured-image-link"> <img src="https://www.sonatype.com/hubfs/RapidResponse%20Mini%20Shai-Hulud.png" alt="Image with text &quot;2,200+ components impacted, mini Shai Hulud hits npm again&quot;" class="hs-featured-image" style="width:auto !important; max-width:50%; float:left; margin:0 15px 15px 0;"> </a> 
</div> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">TL;DR</h2> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p><span>A new wave of the Shai-Hulud malicious package campaign emerged on npm, with </span><a href="https://guide.sonatype.com/vulnerability/sonatype-2026-005579" style="text-decoration: none;">2,225 software component versions</a><span> impacted.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>The malware executes through a malicious preinstall hook, steals npm, GitHub, cloud, Kubernetes, Vault, CI/CD, and other credentials, then uses stolen publishing access to compromise additional packages.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Organizations that installed an affected version should treat the environment as potentially compromised. Remove the malware and any persistence before revoking credentials, then rebuild from known-good components.</span></p> </li> 
</ul> 
<p><span>On August 4, 2026, Shai-Hulud re-emerged in the keyv and cacheable ecosystems on npm, quickly expanding into packages controlled by other maintainers, including packages in the @servicetitan namespace.</span></p> 
<p><span>The affected releases use trusted packages to deliver credential-stealing malware and propagate into additional npm components. The package may be legitimate while the release is not.</span></p> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">What Happened?</h2> 
<p>Attackers publis<span style="text-decoration: none;">hed </span><a href="https://www.ox.security/blog/a-new-infostealer-worm-hits-npm-affecting-keyv-and-cacheable/" style="text-decoration: none;">malicious versions of legitimate npm packages</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> throu</span>gh a compromised GitHub maintainer account and additional publishing accounts reached using stolen credentials, including accounts with access to packages in the @servicetitan namespace. The affected releases <a href="https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-is-back-august/" style="text-decoration: none;">contain a malicious preinstall hook</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> tha</span>t invokes setup.mjs.</p> 
<p><span>Where dependency lifecycle scripts are permitted, the loader downloads a standalone Bun runtime and executes an obfuscated second-stage payload identified as Math_Symbol.js or Math_Init.js. npm 12 blocks unapproved dependency install scripts by default, but the hook can still execute in earlier npm versions or environments configured to permit it.</span></p> 
<p><span>The package can continue working as expected while the surrounding environment is compromised. The malware searches local files, environment variables, running processes, cloud metadata services, Kubernetes service accounts, and Vault locations for npm, GitHub, cloud, CI/CD, database, SSH, payment, messaging, and other credentials.</span></p> 
<p><span>It then encrypts and exfiltrates the collected data. When it finds usable npm publishing access, it identifies other packages controlled by the victim, injects the same malicious hook and payload, increments their versions, and republishes them.</span></p> 
<p><span>That creates a repeatable cycle:</span></p> 
<ol> 
 <li> <p><span>Compromise a trusted maintainer or publishing credential.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Publish malware through a legitimate package.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Steal credentials from a developer machine or CI environment.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Use those credentials to compromise more packages.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Repeat.</span></p> </li> 
</ol> 
<p><span>The use of Bun adds another layer to the execution chain and may help the payload operate beyond controls focused narrowly on Node.js. Relevant activity can include node running setup.mjs, downloads of a Bun archive, Bun executing Math_Symbol.js or Math_Init.js, temporary Bun files, and unexpected outbound traffic to npm, GitHub, cloud metadata services, or attacker-controlled infrastructure.</span></p> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">How Shai-Hulud Persists and Evolves</h2> 
<p>Th<span style="text-decoration: none;">e </span><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/ongoing-npm-software-supply-chain-attack-exposes-new-risks" style="text-decoration: none;">original Shai-Hulud campaign</a><span style="text-decoration: none;">, f</span>irst observed in September 2025, demonstrated that malicious npm packages could do more than steal secrets.</p> 
<p>This campaign follows the defining behav<span style="text-decoration: none;">ior of </span><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/shai-hulud-is-back-maintainers-the-target" style="text-decoration: none;">the Shai-Hulud malware family</a><span style="text-decoration: none;">: com</span>promise trusted packages, harvest credentials, abuse publishing access, and propagate through the open source ecosystem.</p> 
<p>Earlier Shai-Hulud npm activity showed that malware could mo<span style="text-decoration: none;">ve </span><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/the-second-coming-of-shai-hulud-attackers-innovating-on-npm" style="text-decoration: none;">beyond one-time credential theft</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> a</span>nd use stolen tokens to poison additional packages. Later <a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/new-shai-hulud-miasma-wave-hits-hundreds-of-npm-packages" style="text-decoration: none;">Miasma waves</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> conti</span>nued to change their execution and obfuscation techniques while preserving that basic model.</p> 
<p><span>Mini Shai-Hulud adds or extends several techniques, including:</span></p> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p><span>Downloading Bun to execute its second stage.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Using separate GitHub and domain-based exfiltration channels.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Targeting AI coding and IDE configuration.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Establishing host-level persistence.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Republishing compromised packages through trusted identities and workflows.</span></p> </li> 
</ul> 
<p>Microsoft Threat Intellige<span style="text-decoration: none;">nce </span><a href="https://x.com/MsftSecIntel/status/2084642457048752134?s=46" style="text-decoration: none;">reported a consistent infection pattern</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> a</span>cross the affected packages it examined, suggesting one actor was using multiple stolen tokens. That does not establish that every Shai-Hulud campaign comes from the same operator, but the technical lineage is difficult to miss</p> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">More Than 2,200 Affected Versions</h2> 
<p>At the time of publication, Sonatype Research Labs is tracking 2,225 component versions associated wi<span style="text-decoration: none;">th </span>sonatype-2026-005579.</p> 
<p><span>Sonatype tracks versions because risk can differ from one release to the next. Teams need to know whether the version they actually use is affected, not simply whether the package name appears on a list.</span></p> 
<p>The count is a current snapshot, not a final tally. Organizations should check their application ex<span style="text-decoration: none;">posure in </span><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/products/sonatype-guide" style="text-decoration: none;">Sonatype Guide</a> or their <a href="https://www.sonatype.com/resources/articles/what-is-software-composition-analysis" style="text-decoration: none;">software composition analysis (SCA)</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> data rather th</span>an rely on an early static package list.</p> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">How Should Organizations Respond?</h2> 
<p><span>Organizations should check developer workstations, CI/CD runners, build agents, caches, container images, and related environments for affected components.</span></p> 
<p><span>Review package.json, package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, SBOMs, build logs, and repository or proxy telemetry. Look for:</span></p> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p><span>setup.mjs, Math_Symbol.js, and Math_Init.js.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Unexpected Bun binaries.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Suspicious changes to .claude/settings.json or .vscode/tasks.json.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Unauthorized npm releases or unusual GitHub repository activity.</span></p> </li> 
</ul> 
<p><span>If an affected version was installed, removing the package is not enough. Isolate the system, preserve relevant logs, investigate outbound activity, and remove any persistence before revoking or rotating potentially exposed npm, GitHub, cloud, Vault, Kubernetes, CI/CD, SSH, database, and service credentials.</span></p> 
<p><span>Then rebuild from a known-clean environment using verified, uncompromised package versions. Do not assume a later version is safe simply because its number is higher.</span></p> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">Trust Is Still the Attack Vector</h2> 
<p><span>The Mini Shai-Hulud npm compromise reinforces a pattern Sonatype continues to track across npm attacks: adversaries are increasingly targeting trusted maintainers, packages, and publishing workflows rather than relying on typosquatting, dependency confusion, or suspicious new package names.</span></p> 
<p><span>Many organizations still make software security decisions based on historical reputation:</span></p> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p><span>The package is popular.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>The maintainer is known.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>The project has existed for years.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Previous versions were safe.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>The release includes provenance.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>The update appears to come from the normal publishing workflow.</span></p> </li> 
</ul> 
<p><span>None of those signals proves that the component being downloaded now is safe.</span></p> 
<p><span>Security teams must verify the specific behavior of incoming component versions rather than relying on historical project trust. They also need proactive controls to intercept malicious components before they execute in developer workstations or build pipelines.</span></p> 
<p><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/sonatype-research-labs" style="text-decoration: none;">Sonatype Research Labs</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> wi</span>ll continue investigating the campaign and updating <a href="https://guide.sonatype.com/vulnerability/sonatype-2026-005579" style="text-decoration: none;">sonatype-2026-005579</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> a</span>s additional components and technical details are confirmed. This follows Sonatype's editorial approach of leading with timely intelligence, grounding conclusions in research, and giving developers and security teams practical next steps.</p></description>
      <content:encoded><div class="hs-featured-image-wrapper"> 
 <a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/mini-shai-hulud-npm-attack-more-than-2200-components-impacted" title="" class="hs-featured-image-link"> <img src="https://www.sonatype.com/hubfs/RapidResponse%20Mini%20Shai-Hulud.png" alt="Image with text &quot;2,200+ components impacted, mini Shai Hulud hits npm again&quot;" class="hs-featured-image" style="width:auto !important; max-width:50%; float:left; margin:0 15px 15px 0;"> </a> 
</div> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">TL;DR</h2> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p><span>A new wave of the Shai-Hulud malicious package campaign emerged on npm, with </span><a href="https://guide.sonatype.com/vulnerability/sonatype-2026-005579" style="text-decoration: none;">2,225 software component versions</a><span> impacted.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>The malware executes through a malicious preinstall hook, steals npm, GitHub, cloud, Kubernetes, Vault, CI/CD, and other credentials, then uses stolen publishing access to compromise additional packages.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Organizations that installed an affected version should treat the environment as potentially compromised. Remove the malware and any persistence before revoking credentials, then rebuild from known-good components.</span></p> </li> 
</ul> 
<p><span>On August 4, 2026, Shai-Hulud re-emerged in the keyv and cacheable ecosystems on npm, quickly expanding into packages controlled by other maintainers, including packages in the @servicetitan namespace.</span></p> 
<p><span>The affected releases use trusted packages to deliver credential-stealing malware and propagate into additional npm components. The package may be legitimate while the release is not.</span></p> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">What Happened?</h2> 
<p>Attackers publis<span style="text-decoration: none;">hed </span><a href="https://www.ox.security/blog/a-new-infostealer-worm-hits-npm-affecting-keyv-and-cacheable/" style="text-decoration: none;">malicious versions of legitimate npm packages</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> throu</span>gh a compromised GitHub maintainer account and additional publishing accounts reached using stolen credentials, including accounts with access to packages in the @servicetitan namespace. The affected releases <a href="https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-is-back-august/" style="text-decoration: none;">contain a malicious preinstall hook</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> tha</span>t invokes setup.mjs.</p> 
<p><span>Where dependency lifecycle scripts are permitted, the loader downloads a standalone Bun runtime and executes an obfuscated second-stage payload identified as Math_Symbol.js or Math_Init.js. npm 12 blocks unapproved dependency install scripts by default, but the hook can still execute in earlier npm versions or environments configured to permit it.</span></p> 
<p><span>The package can continue working as expected while the surrounding environment is compromised. The malware searches local files, environment variables, running processes, cloud metadata services, Kubernetes service accounts, and Vault locations for npm, GitHub, cloud, CI/CD, database, SSH, payment, messaging, and other credentials.</span></p> 
<p><span>It then encrypts and exfiltrates the collected data. When it finds usable npm publishing access, it identifies other packages controlled by the victim, injects the same malicious hook and payload, increments their versions, and republishes them.</span></p> 
<p><span>That creates a repeatable cycle:</span></p> 
<ol> 
 <li> <p><span>Compromise a trusted maintainer or publishing credential.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Publish malware through a legitimate package.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Steal credentials from a developer machine or CI environment.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Use those credentials to compromise more packages.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Repeat.</span></p> </li> 
</ol> 
<p><span>The use of Bun adds another layer to the execution chain and may help the payload operate beyond controls focused narrowly on Node.js. Relevant activity can include node running setup.mjs, downloads of a Bun archive, Bun executing Math_Symbol.js or Math_Init.js, temporary Bun files, and unexpected outbound traffic to npm, GitHub, cloud metadata services, or attacker-controlled infrastructure.</span></p> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">How Shai-Hulud Persists and Evolves</h2> 
<p>Th<span style="text-decoration: none;">e </span><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/ongoing-npm-software-supply-chain-attack-exposes-new-risks" style="text-decoration: none;">original Shai-Hulud campaign</a><span style="text-decoration: none;">, f</span>irst observed in September 2025, demonstrated that malicious npm packages could do more than steal secrets.</p> 
<p>This campaign follows the defining behav<span style="text-decoration: none;">ior of </span><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/shai-hulud-is-back-maintainers-the-target" style="text-decoration: none;">the Shai-Hulud malware family</a><span style="text-decoration: none;">: com</span>promise trusted packages, harvest credentials, abuse publishing access, and propagate through the open source ecosystem.</p> 
<p>Earlier Shai-Hulud npm activity showed that malware could mo<span style="text-decoration: none;">ve </span><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/the-second-coming-of-shai-hulud-attackers-innovating-on-npm" style="text-decoration: none;">beyond one-time credential theft</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> a</span>nd use stolen tokens to poison additional packages. Later <a href="https://www.sonatype.com/blog/new-shai-hulud-miasma-wave-hits-hundreds-of-npm-packages" style="text-decoration: none;">Miasma waves</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> conti</span>nued to change their execution and obfuscation techniques while preserving that basic model.</p> 
<p><span>Mini Shai-Hulud adds or extends several techniques, including:</span></p> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p><span>Downloading Bun to execute its second stage.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Using separate GitHub and domain-based exfiltration channels.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Targeting AI coding and IDE configuration.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Establishing host-level persistence.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Republishing compromised packages through trusted identities and workflows.</span></p> </li> 
</ul> 
<p>Microsoft Threat Intellige<span style="text-decoration: none;">nce </span><a href="https://x.com/MsftSecIntel/status/2084642457048752134?s=46" style="text-decoration: none;">reported a consistent infection pattern</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> a</span>cross the affected packages it examined, suggesting one actor was using multiple stolen tokens. That does not establish that every Shai-Hulud campaign comes from the same operator, but the technical lineage is difficult to miss</p> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">More Than 2,200 Affected Versions</h2> 
<p>At the time of publication, Sonatype Research Labs is tracking 2,225 component versions associated wi<span style="text-decoration: none;">th </span>sonatype-2026-005579.</p> 
<p><span>Sonatype tracks versions because risk can differ from one release to the next. Teams need to know whether the version they actually use is affected, not simply whether the package name appears on a list.</span></p> 
<p>The count is a current snapshot, not a final tally. Organizations should check their application ex<span style="text-decoration: none;">posure in </span><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/products/sonatype-guide" style="text-decoration: none;">Sonatype Guide</a> or their <a href="https://www.sonatype.com/resources/articles/what-is-software-composition-analysis" style="text-decoration: none;">software composition analysis (SCA)</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> data rather th</span>an rely on an early static package list.</p> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">How Should Organizations Respond?</h2> 
<p><span>Organizations should check developer workstations, CI/CD runners, build agents, caches, container images, and related environments for affected components.</span></p> 
<p><span>Review package.json, package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, SBOMs, build logs, and repository or proxy telemetry. Look for:</span></p> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p><span>setup.mjs, Math_Symbol.js, and Math_Init.js.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Unexpected Bun binaries.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Suspicious changes to .claude/settings.json or .vscode/tasks.json.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Unauthorized npm releases or unusual GitHub repository activity.</span></p> </li> 
</ul> 
<p><span>If an affected version was installed, removing the package is not enough. Isolate the system, preserve relevant logs, investigate outbound activity, and remove any persistence before revoking or rotating potentially exposed npm, GitHub, cloud, Vault, Kubernetes, CI/CD, SSH, database, and service credentials.</span></p> 
<p><span>Then rebuild from a known-clean environment using verified, uncompromised package versions. Do not assume a later version is safe simply because its number is higher.</span></p> 
<h2 style="font-size: 30px; font-weight: normal;">Trust Is Still the Attack Vector</h2> 
<p><span>The Mini Shai-Hulud npm compromise reinforces a pattern Sonatype continues to track across npm attacks: adversaries are increasingly targeting trusted maintainers, packages, and publishing workflows rather than relying on typosquatting, dependency confusion, or suspicious new package names.</span></p> 
<p><span>Many organizations still make software security decisions based on historical reputation:</span></p> 
<ul> 
 <li> <p><span>The package is popular.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>The maintainer is known.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>The project has existed for years.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>Previous versions were safe.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>The release includes provenance.</span></p> </li> 
 <li> <p><span>The update appears to come from the normal publishing workflow.</span></p> </li> 
</ul> 
<p><span>None of those signals proves that the component being downloaded now is safe.</span></p> 
<p><span>Security teams must verify the specific behavior of incoming component versions rather than relying on historical project trust. They also need proactive controls to intercept malicious components before they execute in developer workstations or build pipelines.</span></p> 
<p><a href="https://www.sonatype.com/sonatype-research-labs" style="text-decoration: none;">Sonatype Research Labs</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> wi</span>ll continue investigating the campaign and updating <a href="https://guide.sonatype.com/vulnerability/sonatype-2026-005579" style="text-decoration: none;">sonatype-2026-005579</a><span style="text-decoration: none;"> a</span>s additional components and technical details are confirmed. This follows Sonatype's editorial approach of leading with timely intelligence, grounding conclusions in research, and giving developers and security teams practical next steps.</p>
